source.title: From Density Matrices to Phase Transitions in Deep Learning: Spectral Early Warnings and Interpretability

record.tranche_reason: The study examines grokking on a modular arithmetic task and measures train/test accuracy and internal progress signals, using a different method from the original grokking studies.
record.gate_note: The grokking accuracy and spectral results are reported in figures without numerical values. Other experiments in the paper concern induction-head formation and emergent misalignment, not delayed generalization as defined by the claim. The PR observation about weight-decay/update balance does not test the efficiency account.
record.test_reason: The paper introduces a detector (the 2RDM, with its spectral heat capacity and participation ratio). It uses grokking on modular division (p=97, 50% split, AdamW, weight decay 1.0, one seed) as a known phase transition to validate that detector. The accuracy curves are shown only as figures, with no stated chance level, final accuracy or delay length. Training-set size is not varied. The Fourier analysis is applied to an eigenvector of the loss covariance, not to the network's weights or circuit. So the grokking results report the method's own signals on a known transition and do not independently test whether any version holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that the 2RDM detects and interprets phase transitions cheaply. For grokking, they claim that the test-block spectral heat capacity spike marks generalizing-circuit formation and that the top eigenvector concentrates on the Fourier modes being learned. Both claims are interpretive, supported by the authors' argument and one seed, without an independent measure of the circuit.
record.recipe_differences: Uses modular division rather than the modular addition example in the claim, with a 50%/50% split, AdamW, strong weight decay, and 2RDM-based measurements of accuracy-linked progress.
record.method_sensitivity: For the grokking measurement, the paper uses fixed training and test probe subsets and a sliding-window covariance; the text does not report outcome comparisons across settings.

fits_no_version.finding: A spike in the test-block spectral heat capacity of the loss covariance precedes the rise in test accuracy. The top eigenvector concentrates on a few 2D Fourier modes (Fig 7b, Fig 8; single seed, figure-only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss-covariance spectral statistics on held-out probes give an early-warning signal for grokking.

fits_no_version.finding: The participation ratio rises, then plateaus when the weight-decay and gradient-update magnitudes balance (Fig 9b).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking training with strong weight decay enters a non-equilibrium steady state that is detectable from the loss-covariance participation ratio.

record.problems: The grokking results use random seed 42, with no uncertainty estimates stated. Accuracy and diagnostic values are presented in figures without numerical values in the text. The paper gives no training-set-size sweep. The grokking setup details disagree on window size: Section G.3 says 40 recordings, while Table 9 says 20.

untested.parts: Delay length, chance-to-near-perfect jump, and how the delay depends on training-set size.
Gradual formation of the Fourier circuit in the weights, later removal of memorization, and progress measures in the sense of the original sources.
The weight-decay/gradient balance is observed only as a participation-ratio plateau. There is no critical dataset size and no ungrokking.

record.verdict_notes: This is a methods paper; grokking serves as a validation testbed. All grokking results come from seed 42 and are given only in figures. The window size is inconsistent: Section G.3 says 40 recordings, while Table 9 and the main text say 20. The probe-set size is 300 (150 train, 150 test). The appendix compares the spectral heat capacity with the local learning coefficient and gradient norm on grokking (Figs 15–16); these are method comparisons, not tests of the claim.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not compare training-set sizes, so it does not test whether smaller training sets require more optimization. It gives no textual accuracy values establishing chance-level test accuracy, near-perfect final test accuracy, or the duration after training accuracy saturates.

The paper measures a Fourier-structured signal and a test-set SHC signal before the test-accuracy rise. It does not directly track gradual formation of the generalizing circuit or show that memorizing components are removed later.
The non-algorithmic experiments do not test grokking-like delayed generalization switched by initialization scale or weight norm.
The LLM fine-tuning experiment does not test delayed generalization during realistic pretraining or fine-tuning.
The study does not test whether low-norm bias selects a more efficient generalizing circuit, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking below that size.
The study does not compare algorithms learned across runs or architectures.
The study does not test whether grokking is caused by optimizer or numerical artifacts.

rows.note: The text establishes the order of the accuracy increases, but does not state numerical accuracy levels or how long test accuracy remains low after training accuracy saturates.
rows.check: Figure-only. The text says only that test accuracy rises after training accuracy. No accuracy levels or delay length are stated, and there is no training-set-size sweep, so the size of the delay cannot be read. It is a validation setup, not a test.

rows.note: The paper interprets this peak as associated with the initial training-accuracy increase.

rows.operation_detail: Computed SHC using the test-sample block of the 2RDM.

rows.check: This is the method's own signal. The link between the test-block spike and the generalizing circuit is argued by the authors, not measured independently. The spike is from one seed, shown only in a figure.
